speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-81, respecting the Canada court of Indian claims.

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext: The purpose of this bill is to put into effect the unanimous recommendation of the joint Senate and House of Commons committee of last session that there be established a court of claims to deal specifically with the B.C. Indian land question and the Oka land question in Quebec, plus other matters.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who has been giving diligent attention to this particular matter, I feel bound to raise the question as to whether a bill of this sort can be introduced by a private member without involving an expenditure of public funds. I have not seen the bill, as will be obvious, but may I make this reservation now and indicate that our concurrence in leave to introduce this bill is subject to that reservation.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext: If I may speak to the point of order raised by the minister, this bill does not involve a charge upon the crown because the court of Indian claims named is in reality the Exchequer Court of Canada. This bill would give additional powers to the exchequer court which it does not now have, in order that it may deal specifically with these problems.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext: Then the possible objection that might be taken to the bill is reserved for consideration when the bill comes up again.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, surely a point of order that goes to the root of the matter as to whether or not the bill is to be received and dealt with by this house on the motion of a private member is one that cannot be postponed. Surely there has to be a determination of that point of order before the bill can be introduced.
It seems to me, therefore, that the better procedure is to leave the motion on the order paper, deal with the point of order and then determine, after the point of order is decided, whether or not the hon. member may have leave to introduce his bill. If the point of order is well taken, then the bill ought not to be received.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member's suggestion points to the better course. I would think, offhand, that the bill could be introduced and read a first time without committing the house to reading it a second time if objection taken later revealed that the bill was not in accordance with the rules of the house. But I think the hon. member for Ottawa West is correct in saying that it would be preferable not to have the bill read the first time by the house if there is some objection to be taken to it in the matter of form.
Therefore I would think that as the bill has not been seen by hon. members of the house it would be preferable to stand the motion until tomorrow, to give hon. members who are interested an opportunity to look at the bill. I have not the bill before me either, and I am therefore in the same position as other hon. members of the house. In fact I could not proceed with the matter without having the bill. I therefore suggest that this motion stand until tomorrow.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may say with respect to this matter that it raises the all-important question as to how hon. gentlemen can see a bill before it is introduced.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may add
a word, as I understand the point of order raised, concisely stated it is as to whether or not this proposed measure requires to be preceded by a motion on the part of the

Income Tax
government because it is a money bill, requiring the advice of the Governor General that he commends it to the house, under the provisions of section 54 of the British North America Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext:
The point taken by the mover of the bill was that it would not be printed and in the hands of hon. members unless the house gave leave to introduce it. That, I think, has some force. First reading of the bill does give permission for the bill to be printed and distributed and, as I indicated earlier, I see no obstacle to taking exception to a bill after it has been read the first time and before it has proceeded to second reading.
If the hon. member has his bill, perhaps the most convenient course would be to allow him to introduce it and have it read for the first time, if the house is agreeable. Then it will be in the hands of hon. members, and if they feel further objection should be taken they will be able to pursue the matter.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS
speechtext:
I understood that the
procedure to be followed by a private member putting forward a bill was to take it up with the law clerk to see whether it was acceptable, whether it met the provisions of section 54 of the British North America Act and, presumably standing order No. 61 of our rules.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH COURT OF INDIAN CLAIMS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND REVISION OF EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: Did I understand Your Honour to say that the house had already given leave? It seems to me that the leave the house might give would take into account the point raised by Your Honour, and if Your Honour feels that the bill should not be introduced until you have had a chance to look at it I doubt very much whether the house would be prepared to give its leave until you have had an opportunity to consider it further.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND REVISION OF EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Your
Honour having decided on what seem to have been the facts in the first case, which are similar to those in this case, it seems to me that you are bound by the decision rendered with regard to the first case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND REVISION OF EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The decision in the first case was altogether different. In that case I had entered a reservation with respect to whether or not the bill, entitled an act respecting the Canada court of Indian claims, could possibly be a measure which did not impose a burden on the public treasury. I felt we should not give first reading to a bill in that form without such a reservation; that we could make up our minds after we had had a chance to look at it.
With respect to this bill Your Honour has made simply a general reservation. I should think that Your Honour would like a chance to look at the bill before it is introduced into the house. This is, as Your Honour pointed out, by its appearance a bulky bill. We had experience last year, I recall, of a bill which purported to amend a statute and then did nothing of the sort; it merely re-enacted it. I do not know what the effect of this bill is. I raised the point at that time that such a bill was not properly before the house.
Your Honour has now said to us, on the basis of a quick look, that this bill does not appear to make any changes in the Income Tax Act. I certainly would not be prepared to give leave to the introduction of the bill about which Your Honour has expressed a

general reservation. Your Honour having expressed that reservation, I certainly think the house should wait until Your Honour reports back to us before deciding whether or not we are prepared to give leave.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND REVISION OF EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may be allowed one word, I must respectfully disagree with what the Minister of Justice has said. The test is not whether the bill is bulky; the test is whether or not it imposes a charge upon the treasury. If it is a charge upon the treasury it seems to me it ought not to be introduced, and Your Honour having ruled in the first instance this seems to me to be a case where Your Honour has to follow the original ruling or upset the ruling in the other case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND REVISION OF EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; with respect the hon. gentleman has missed the point. No one was raising a point of order on this bill with respect to whether or not it was a charge on the treasury. That point is not raised here. But as Your Honour, looking at it, has expressed a reservation whether or not the bill is, generally speaking, in proper form, since the leave of the house is not a matter which should be automatically given, I think the house would wish to take the position that we do not give our leave until Your Honour has had the opportunity to report to us further on the bill for which leave is now sought.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND REVISION OF EXISTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:

This is rather a difficult choice for the house to make without having seen the bill.

In the circumstances I think I will do what has been said. I am obliged to proceed to the next stage and put the matter before the house by putting the motion.

DEVELOPED COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext: Has the external aid office in hand, or under consideration, any program of teaching assistance for undeveloped countries of the commonwealth, which would centre on the use of Canadian secondary, vocational, and university teachers in a crash, summer program, taking advantage of holiday release in Canada: and, if not, why not?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEVELOPED COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES
speechtext:
The requests which have been received from the less developed commonwealth countries for assistance from Canada in the teaching field have all been for persons who are prepared to serve abroad for a year or more. The cost of sending teachers overseas for short periods would be very high in relation to the assistance they could render in a limited period, and Canadian teachers would probably require a disproportionate amount of time during a short assignment to become familiar with local conditions. For these reasons the external aid office is not contemplating at present a program of the kind referred to and it is considered that the funds available for this form of Canadian assistance can be more effectively used in meeting requests for teachers for longer assignments.

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO LORD'S DAY ACT
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Is it the intention of the government to introduce at this session amendments to the Lord's Day Act?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO LORD'S DAY ACT
speechtext: Representations on this subject have been received from time to time, and these representations indicate clearly that views as to what changes should be made vary very widely depending on the area from which they come and also on the traditions and background of the organization or individual from whom they are received. This whole question has been carefully considered, both in general and in the light of individual representations, and the conclusion is that it would not be appropriate or desirable to bring in amendments to the Lord's Day Act at the present session.

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO LORD'S DAY ACT
speechtext: A supplementary question, if I may. Has any such consideration taken into account the question of coin operated laundries and other activities which are of vital importance on the eve of the opening of the 1962 tourist season?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF AMENDMENTS TO LORD'S DAY ACT
speechtext:
Yes, these considerations have taken into account the situation with regard to coin operated laundries and other activities. The scheme of the Lord's Day Act is that the basic law respecting Sunday observance is of general application but variations from the general law may be enacted by the provincial legislatures so as to reflect regional or local views and requirements in respect of particular activities. Thus the provincial legislatures may, under section 4 of the act, provide exemptions from the prohibition against the transaction of business on Sunday, and under section 6 provide exemptions from the prohibition against conducting games and performances where an admission fee is charged. The situation with regard to coin operated laundries and other coin operated machines would appear to be essentially one that can be more suitably dealt with on a local basis by

Inquiries of the Ministry the provincial legislatures, which are now all in session, without making an amendment of general application to the Lord's Day Act.

The provision for a chief judge is one which personally commends itself to me, and I think will commend itself to the house, as a measure which is being introduced into the administration of the system of courts in Ontario designed to further the better and more expeditious dispatch of business in those district and county courts. In Alberta, for instance, there is a similar provision which has been in existence for some time. There are, in fact, two chief judges there, one of the northern and one of the southern districts. They direct in general the operation of the courts within those districts, and the system has worked well and efficiently.
With respect to the trial division of the high court, hon. members will be aware, of course, of the recent appointment of Mr. Justice Wilson as chief justice of Cyprus, an appointment which brings honour and credit to Canada and its judiciary as well as to the judge himself. Mr. Justice Wilson has accordingly been granted leave of absence without pay. It is anticipated that his appointment will last for six years. This then leaves the high court short one judge for

that period, and this situation will be taken care of by one portion of the amendment now before the committee. In addition there is in my view need for a further judge, so that the amendment provides for two additional judges of the high court.
As hon. members will see when it is distributed, if the committee approves the resolution, the bill will be in the standard form of a bill for this purpose with the exception only that it will come into force on proclamation. The reason for this provision is that there is some urgency about this situation. I was advised by the attorney general of Ontario that they were in fact proceeding with the introduction of the necessary legislation into their house, and I was requested to make the necessary provision here as soon as possible. Normally we wait until the legislation has gone through the provincial legislature before introducing it here. In view of the representations I received and with which I concur as to the urgency of providing these additional appointments, I undertook to introduce our legislation at once on the basis that we would insert the provision for proclamation so that it would not go into effect until after the appropriate legislation has gone through the Ontario house.
That legislation has been introduced. I am not certain whether it has yet been carried, but I understand it is well on its way through the Ontario legislature.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL ONTARIO JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think hon. members will agree that with the growth in population of the province of Ontario and the accompanying increase in business and volume of litigation, it is necessary that there be some addition to the judiciary. Whether the figure should be two additional judges of the trial division of the supreme court of Ontario, or one or three or five, I would consider something that could be argued at great length and I do not propose to do that at the moment, because it would appear, at least on the surface, that two is a reasonable number as it relates to the present constitution of that court.
The additional judges being provided for the county and district courts of the province are required not only because of the growth to which I have referred but also because of the increase in jurisdiction of the county courts. To the extent that that increase in jurisdiction takes away work from the trial division of the supreme court it has a bearing on the number to be added to the trial division of the supreme court and, of course, on the number of county judges to be added.
The situation in the county court judiciary has not been a happy one for some years,
Judges Act
basically because of the fact that in some counties in which there is a large population the work load has increased rapidly, while in other counties the work load has remained static or has decreased. Not always has the rearrangement of the service of the county court judges and the making of them available to certain of the cities in which the increase has been large kept pace with the changes in the distribution of population within the province. A real problem exists there, but it is largely within the jurisdiction of the province. As far as the federal authority is concerned, it can merely provide the number of judges required by the province. Areal problem exists there but as I say, it is largely the concern of the provinces. However, it is one which perhaps needs more thorough attention than it is getting.
Basically, for the older part of Ontario, the boundaries of the counties are those which were set up some 114 years ago. There has been little significant change in them since that time. Hence some real problems exist. However, as I say, they are within the jurisdiction of the provinces and I therefore do not propose to develop a discussion on them other than to indicate the nature of the problem. I mention it here in the hope that it will receive more consideration than it has received in the past.
There is one other question that arises out of this resolution. I think all hon. members will agree that under our system of government, respect for the judiciary is of the utmost importance. By and large over the years our reputation in this country for having a competent, wholly impartial, hard working and fair judiciary is very good. I think all hon. members will agree that is the case by and large in the country. However, a situation is developing here which requires us to ask ourselves this question. What is the use of increasing the number of judges if the situation among them, by reason of inadequacy of pay, is such that we are not going to have the best persons available for appointment to fill these vacancies? That is a question on which I feel very strongly, and it is one that is germane to this particular resolution.
The county court judges' salaries have not been increased since 1955. They are substantially below those of most of the solicitors in the minister's own department, except the very junior ones. The legislation requires that a county court judge, to be eligible for appointment, must have 10 years' experience in practising his profession. Yet we pay him on a lower basis than that on which we pay his counterpart who enters the civil service as a junior out of law school. We may well

Judges Act
ask ourselves whether it is serving any useful purpose to increase the number of the judiciary if we are going to leave the other half of the problem undealt with and the situation such that the government cannot get the type of competent, experienced personnel required to accept these appointments.
The situation with respect to the trial division of the supreme court of Ontario is equally bad. It is now a case of a person appointed to this division having to take a reduction in earnings in order to accept the appointment. The pay level is such that if these persons have a family at a stage where they are seeking to educate them, it is impossible for them to take the appointment unless they have outside means.
That is not a desirable situation. It means that in considering persons for appointment the government have available to them only older men who are past the stage of active practice and are looking to the appointment as an end to their professional careers rather than as an opportunity for undertaking great new work which should be held in the highest repute in the profession, as indeed it is. That situation is one that causes a good deal of alarm at the present time.
I was happy to hear the minister make reference to the appointment of one of the members of the trial division of the supreme court of Ontario to the position of chief justice of Cyprus. That appointment tends to emphasize the high repute in which our judiciary have been held in the past in this country, and indicates the background of the general reputation of the judiciary in the province. I would hope that the minister would see fit to deal with this matter of the inadequacy of pay of the judiciary so that the high reputation which has been enjoyed up to the present time by our judiciary can be continued in the future and so that, by reason of inadequacy of pay, he will not be obliged to appoint persons with lesser qualifications than we would wish them to have.
It seems to me that respect for the judiciary is an inherent part of the effective function of our whole system of government. That being so we must by our legislation, and the government by its action, take all steps that will ensure that the judiciary will command that respect. If we are to continue the underpayment of the judiciary, as we are doing now, we are in danger of appointing persons who are less well qualified and who will not command that respect which the judiciary has always had.
I might add that I am somewhat at a loss to understand why this urgent problem has not been dealt with, particularly in view of the fact that at least two major upward revisions of public service salaries and pension

legislation have taken place since the judges' salaries were last examined. No explanation at all has been given as to why this deplorable omission has occurred. I ask the minister to explain, before the resolution carries, how he hopes to have a relatively wide choice of qualified persons for consideration for appointment on the present pay level. I would hope that he would give a thoroughgoing answer to that problem.

This takes them away from their judicial work, and a very nice question arises as to whether county judges should be encouraged to do that sort of thing in order to earn a living.
It is not desirable, from the point of view of judicial work, that they be taken from that judicial work to perform these other duties which, in the main, are connected with labour disputes but may relate to other types of arbitration as well. As a matter of fact I believe the trade unions call this practice of having two jobs moonlighting. I do not believe this practice is helpful in maintaining the kind of standard in the profession that it is desirable and indeed necessary to maintain. I interpret the minister's explanation as an additional reason for dealing with the question of judicial salaries promptly.
I thank the minister for his explanation about proclaiming the act, which I take it from his remarks will come into force upon receiving royal assent rather than at a date to be set by proclamation. This raises a very interesting proposition. It means that the minister is coming before this committee and
Judges Act
asking us to pass legislation that may never be required. In other words he is dealing with this legislation in quite a different manner than the accepted practice. The accepted practice has been for the province to pass the necessary provincial legislation setting up the requirement for additional judges; then the federal authority makes provision for the appointment of those judges. The minister wants now to reverse the practice without an adequate reason.
There are a great many conjectures one could make as to his reasons for adopting an improper practice of this type and taking up the time of the committee in passing legislation that may never be required. This government has been raising at all times recently and even earlier today, the question of wasting time in this house, so I feel it exceeding strange that the minister should be making this request. Perhaps the minister should plead guilty at once to wasting the time of the house by presenting the legislation that may never be required.
Be that as it may, I think a more practical reason for the introduction of this measure in this unusual way is that the minister fears dissolution of the house, and would like to make the appointments before dissolution knowing that the government will be changed. If I make more assumptions on that subject I may be ruled out of order by the Chair; however, I suggest perhaps that is the real reason for the minister proceeding in this improper way. I must say that this is one of the best examples we have had of a government, which complains about the time of the house being taken up improperly, taking up the time of the house improperly itself. the second reading of Bill No. C-38, to provide for the reporting of financial and other statistics relating to the affairs of corporations and labour unions carrying on activities in Canada.
He said: The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is "to provide for the reporting of financial and other statistics relating to the affairs of corporations and labour unions carrying on activities in Canada." The speech from the throne mentioned that parliament would be asked to consider legislation on this subject during the present session.
This is an extremely important bill, and it forms an integral part of the government's national policy. Canadians are becoming increasingly aware of their nationhood and of the importance of developing to the full the cultural, social and economic resources of this country. This bill is directly related to the efforts the government has been making in such fields as the domiciling of our constitution in Canada, and also to the numerous steps the government has already taken, and is taking, to encourage the development of the nation's resources, their control by Canadians and their use primarily for the benefit of Canada.
This bill, then, is not a manifestation of any narrow nationalism, nor is it anti-American. It represents the determination of the government to understand fully the operation of our economy, the extent of foreign control of various units operating within that economy, and the effects of that control; and our desire to see that the Canadian people are made aware, in general terms, of these facts and their implications. This is the duty of any responsible government, and this is the basis on which the bill has been drawn up.
The right hon. Prime Minister, as leader of the opposition, on February 11, 1957 when moving the adoption by this house of a natural resources development policy, spoke of the need at that time for:
-a national policy: not a policy of nationalism but one whereby Canada in the days ahead will remain an independent Canada and will not inexorably drift into economic continentalism; one whereby Canada will maintain her economic independence and her sovereignty; a policy that will provide national development for a greater Canada in which growth and prosperity will not

be purchased at the expense of our economic independence and our effective national sovereignty.
The Prime Minister and other ministers have emphasized on many occasions that this national policy is not designed to hamper in any way those investors outside Canada who may wish to devote their capital to the development of Canadian resources and industries. This country needs foreign capital, and will continue to welcome it as long as its activities in Canada are compatible with Canada's national interest.
In this connection the Prime Minister, addressing the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Great Britain, stated succinctly what the government, and indeed Canadians generally, expect of business organizations controlled from outside Canada. He said:
We have made it clear that we expect foreign concerns operating in Canada, or Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies, to carry on operations as Canadian businesses. We expect them to make available a fair portion of their equity securities for purchase by Canadians; to include Canadians on their boards of directors; to make proper disclosure of their Canadian operations; to employ competent Canadians in senior management and technical positions; to conduct a fair share of their research in Canada; to purchase their requirements within Canada if those are available on competitive terms; and not to be denied by those in control a fair opportunity to sell their Canadian products in export markets.
One reason for the fundamental importance of this proposed legislation is the extent of foreign investment in the Canadian economy. Total non-resident investment in Canada as of 1959 amounted to no less than $20.7 billion. In December, 1957, the most recent date for which these figures are available, more than half of all Canadian manufacturing industry- 56 per cent to be precise-was under nonresident control, as were 76 per cent of Canada's petroleum and natural gas industry and 61 per cent of our mining and smelting industry. Altogether there are an estimated 6,500 foreign controlled companies in Canada.
Obviously any sovereign nation must have access to financial information on the operations of industry within its borders. Foreign investment in Canada is so extensive and has such a far reaching effect upon the national economy that information on its activities is essential to the conduct of public affairs. We cordially invite foreign capital to help us with the development of our great natural resources, and we invite foreign investors to derive a profit from this development. Is it not reasonable, therefore, that we should ask them to tell us something about their activities and finances? The proposed legislation seeks, among its various objectives, to fill this gap.

The legislation is also important to the individual Canadian citizen. The government has been urging Canadians to invest their savings in the economic development of their country. But the freedom to buy shares in a developmental or industrial enterprise may be of little value to the private citizen unless he knows something of the nature of the enterprise and of its corporate structure and ownership. He already has access to this information for dominion public companies. He may or may not have access to a company's prospectus filed with a stock exchange. The proposed legislation would make general background data available on all kinds of companies operating in Canada.
Up to this point I have been speaking of corporations, but similar considerations apply to international labour unions. In a sovereign nation it is only to be expected that foreign controlled labour organizations should also divulge general information on their affairs in this country.
Members of the house will recall that last year a bill to provide for returns from corporations and labour unions received first reading.
Following its introduction various representations were received from both companies and unions. For example, it was suggested that the original bill was discriminatory as between various kinds of companies. To remedy this, some suggested that the coverage of the bill should be more restricted, and others that it should be made to apply to all companies. Similarly as related to labour unions, some urged the broadening and others the narrowing of the coverage. It was also stated by some that the original bill would have required companies to lay bare their confidential company affairs before the eyes of their competitors.
Perhaps it was not surprising that representations should have been received or that some of the suggested changes were directly in conflict with others. After all, the bill was the first attempt at legislation in a new and exceedingly complex field. The government therefore welcomed the expression of views by representatives of companies and unions, and these views were very carefully and exhaustively studied and taken into account in the preparation of the new bill.
The measure now proposed, Mr. Speaker, is similar to its predecessor in most respects, but there are five important differences. First, the reporting requirement in the new bill will in general apply to all companies, whether owned or controlled in Canada or abroad, and whether public or private. The bill makes a number of specific exclusions, principally small companies and companies already reporting similar information to the government 26207-1-153
Corporations and Labour Unions under some other statute. Second, all labour unions will be required to make returns whether or not their headquarters are situated outside Canada. Third, the range of information to be reported has been considerably extended as compared with that in the previous bill, in order to give a clearer picture of the extent and particularly the effect of foreign control. Fourth, the information is segregated into two clearly defined classes. The first class will include information that will be available to the public; the second class, which will be for government use only, will include those items whose public disclosure could be damaging to companies competitively. I shall return to this point. Fifth, the initial year for reporting will be 1962 instead of 1960, as in the previous bill. This change should make it appreciably easier for companies and unions to prepare their first returns.
As to the form of the legislation, one possible course might have been to amend the dominion Companies Act. The government, after all, already receives periodic returns from all public companies incorporated under that act, including both Canadian controlled and foreign controlled companies. These reports are filed with the Department of the Secretary of State. It was decided not to use the dominion Companies Act for the present purpose because that act applies only to enterprises incorporated under federal charter and does not cover, for example, the many companies incorporated under provincial charter or licensed by a province, nor does it cover labour unions. The scope of the reporting would therefore have been much too fragmentary.
Instead it was decided that new legislation should be drafted under the authority of head 6 of section 91 of the British North America Act, which authorizes the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to "the census and statistics", so as to permit the collection of financial information pertaining to all firms whether incorporated under federal or other authority, and also of all labour unions.
I have already mentioned that the second question, "Who should be required to report?" presented some difficulty. One possibility might have been to exempt Canadian owned and controlled companies and unions from the reporting requirement. This, however, was felt to be impractical. After all, there are many different means and degrees of control, and it was not considered realistic to single

Corporations and Labour Unions out for exception general classes of corporations such as all private companies or all Canadian owned companies.
Furthermore, on the matter of share ownership for example, the government is interested not only in those corporations having, say 51 per cent of their shares held outside Canada, but also in those having smaller percentages owned abroad; because it is quite possible that effective control may be exercised by the holding of less than 50 per cent of the shares. Similar considerations apply to the various other criteria of control. I should add that information on an across the board basis may be expected to provide useful data to enable comparisons to be made between foreign controlled and Canadian controlled companies, as a broad factual background for the consideration of policy problems that may arise from time to time in this field.
For administrative reasons the reporting requirement will not apply to corporations whose gross revenue during a reporting period was not over $500,000 and whose assets did not exceed $250,000. Companies operating under the authority of such statutes as the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, the Trust Companies Act, the Loan Companies Act, the Small Loans Act, the Radio Act and the Railway Act will also be exempted so as to avoid duplication of returns in cases where already substantially the same kind of information is being obtained under other federal legislation.
In much the same way the legislation would apply to every labour union in Canada having 100 or more members resident in Canada. This requirement to make returns to a public authority is not a new obligation for international unions. The labour management reporting and disclosure act of 1959 in the United States requires all labour organizations to file annual financial reports, a copy of their constitution and various other particulars. Also for some years all union headquarters in Canada have voluntarily given certain information to the Department of Labour, including items such as the names of their officers and the extent of their Canadian membership. This information is published annually by that department in its booklet "Labour Organization in Canada". The returns required by this bill will amplify this information in important respects.
On this third question, "What information should be reported?", the government considered that the requirement should call for only such information as is necessary to give a clear picture of operations in Canada and of the nature of management, ownership and


financial affairs. It is believed that corporations and unions will find the terms of the requirement to be reasonable and no more onerous than is necessary.
One important thing that I would like to emphasize is that the bill is designed to produce factual or statistical replies, rather than value judgments, from respondents. It is a fact finding bill. Questions calling for statements of opinion are avoided. No questions are asked relating to contractual arrangements through which control may be exercised, because of the intangible nature and infinite possible gradations of such control. There are no direct questions concerning company procurement policy, personnel policy, investment policy or export policy. The bill does not ask companies to identify their "beneficial" shareholders, because it is recognized that in many cases this information is not available to the companies themselves. The government is concerned primarily with the incidence and extent of foreign ownership and with the effects of foreign ownership on a factual basis, and intends through this bill to provide a basis on which further studies may be made, as may be necessary, on particular aspects of such ownership or control.
I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, that the returns will be divided into confidential and non-confidential sections. The non-confidential items to be reported by corporations will include information as to how and when they were incorporated, the amount of their authorized share capital, the number of shares held by persons having addresses of record within Canada or elsewhere, the name and address of any corporation holding 10 per cent or more of any class of share, the total amount of debentures issued and outstanding, and the name, address and nationality of each director and officer.
Section B, the confidential part of the return, will include financial statements and an itemized statement showing separately certain payments made by the corporation in the reporting period to persons not resident in Canada. This will include remittances abroad covering such items as dividends, interest, rent, royalties, fees, salaries and other charges as against the operation in Canada. It will be appreciated, therefore, on examination of the bill, that section B can be said generally to be devoted to producing information designed to give in a factual way an idea as to the effect on the operation within Canada of the foreign control, whereas section A of the return is designed to give us factual information as to the physical extent of the foreign control of those corporations operating within Canada, and the same with respect to

labour unions. It will be appreciated, therefore, that with respect to part B the very nature of the information desired indicates it to be of a confidential nature and, further, that it might be of immense value to competitors who would find it for the first time.
Labour unions affected by the legislation will be required to provide similar kinds of information, also divided into the two parts. In section A they will furnish a copy of their constitution, name and address of each local union or branch in Canada, information on trusteeships, a list of employers in Canada with whom they have a collective agreement; and the name, address and nationality of each officer and employee of the union resident in Canada-with the obvious exception of clerks and stenographers-together with information on the manner of selection or appointment of these persons. Section B, the confidential part of the return, will include the union's financial statements and a classified statement showing separately the amounts paid to a union with headquarters outside Canada by members resident in Canada on account of initiation fees, membership dues, health and welfare assessments, death benefit assessments, strike benefit assessments, fines and work permits.
In preparing the legislation, particular care has been taken to ensure that unnecessary information is not being requested, and that the burden of reporting will not be relatively more onerous for labour unions than for corporations, or vice versa, having regard to the differences in their functions. As a further means of facilitating the preparation of the reports, it is contemplated that corporations will be permitted to file financial statements in the same form and at the same time as those supplied to the Department of National Revenue for income tax purposes. This relates only to the general statements such as the balance sheet, statement of income and expenditure, and statement of surplus; copies of the detailed and confidential schedules filed for income tax purposes will not be required by this bill. As still another means of simplification, the bill contains a special provision whereby certain information will not have to be filed year after year.
I have spoken of the kinds of information to be obtained, and I should like now to turn to the use to be made of it. The bill provides that the non-confidential part-section A- of the return filed by each corporation shall be kept on record in an office of the Department of the Secretary of State, and that section A of the return by each union shall be held by the Department of Labour. Any person will be permitted to inspect these reports upon payment of a nominal fee not exceeding 26207-1-153J
Corporations and Labour Unions $1 in respect of any one corporation or union. This fee is intended merely to cover the government's costs of recording and indexing the returns and of providing facilities for their inspection by the interested persons.
Section B of any return filed by either a corporation or a union will be privileged information, and will not be available to any person other than an official or authorized person, nor for any purpose except a purpose relating to the administration of this act.
At this point, I think I should indicate certain changes which will be proposed in the detailed operation of this legislation. These changes arise largely from the consideration we have given to a number of representations we have received since this bill was introduced.
First, it was suggested that since it is im- 1 portant that the confidential parts of the reports be kept strictly confidential, they should not be required to be filed with the Departments of the Secretary of State and of Labour respectively, but with an organization which, from the very nature of its operations and functions, is accustomed to the receipt and custody of confidential statistics.
It was represented to us that industry and business, as well as unions, are anxious to co-operate with the government in carrying out the purposes of this bill, and that the business segment especially would find it much more acceptable from this point of view if the returns were to be filed with the dominion bureau of statistics, which has established an enviable reputation, and has the trust and confidence of all those who are required to furnish returns to it.
I may say that in my view, and that of the government, the fears expressed by those who made those representations to us as to the dangers that the confidential parts of the returns might get into unauthorized hands and be used for unauthorized purposes under the bill as drafted, were, to say the least, somewhat exaggerated. However, the bill is to some extent experimental and it is, indeed, as I myself recognize, a first step. Certainly, its successful operation does depend upon good relations and mutual confidence between the government and those who are filing returns if we are to get the full and frank disclosure which is desirable. Therefore, we felt that in view of these considerations no harm, certainly, would be done by giving effect to these representations which we had received.
Accordingly, it has been decided that all returns, both part A and part B, should be made in the first instance to the dominion statistician. The dominion statistician will in

Corporations and Labour Unions turn forward one copy of part A of the company returns to the Secretary of State, and one copy of part A of the union returns to the Minister of Labour. Those portions of the returns will be available for inspection in those respective departments in the same manner and circumstances as is now provided in the bill. Part B of the returns will remain in the control and custody of the dominion statistician.
With respect to part B of the returns, the use to be made of them will remain, in general, as now provided, subject to the observations I shall make in a few moments. That is to say, the details may not be made public at any time, but they will be processed and analysed in the bureau and the general effect and conclusions to be drawn therefrom will be published in the form of an annual report for the information of the public, but framed in such a manner that individual statistics and information cannot be identified or related to any individual corporation or union making returns.
I should emphasize that this new obligation imposed on the bureau of statistics, and the method of dealing with the returns received, does not imply any departure from the rules and procedures now applying with respect to returns received under the Statistics Act.
Next, it has been suggested that there is a danger, as the bill is presently drawn, that confidential information contained in the returns will somehow fall into the hands of persons by whom it will be used for purposes not connected with the bill.
Suspicion has even fallen on the Minister of Justice for no better reason, apparently, than that he has the carriage of the bill through the house, although no return will ever be made to him under the bill. Here again we feel that these fears are somewhat exaggerated, to say the least. The provisions of the act now carefully define who is an authorized person and limit the uses that such persons may make of any information received. To act in the manner that some have suggested would be done would clearly be a breach of the statute. However, once again we recognize that it is essential that there be co-operation and confidence, if there is to be full disclosure and advantage from the legislation.
I would have been prepared, therefore, in any event, if there appeared in this house to be any feeling that it would be desirable to amend the bill to make it even more abundantly clear that information could not be communicated or used as suggested, to accept an appropriate amendment to clause 14, As it is, now that it has been decided in any event to use the bureau of statistics, and


in view of the desirability of preserving intact the tradition of non-disclosure to unauthorized persons or for unauthorized purposes of any information the bureau has received, I believe it would be advisable to modify clause 14 to reflect absolutely this position. Accordingly, at the appropriate stage, I shall ask one of my colleagues to move the appropriate amendments. There will be a fair number of consequential amendments arising from the foregoing decisions which I shall also ask one of my colleagues to move at the appropriate points in committee of the whole.
I should like to emphasize again, Mr. Speaker, that the financial information in section B of the individual reports which might affect the relationship between competitors will remain strictly confidential. It is to be used only for the purposes of this act and may not be used, for example, as a cross check for the purposes of other acts such as the Income Tax Act or the Combines Investigation Act.
The bill makes provision, also, for any necessary regulations, and for penalties for failure to file a return for a reporting period as required by the act, or for improperly divulging confidential information.
This legislation will provide the government and the citizens with basic information on corporations and labour unions operating in this country supplementing the limited data heretofore available. We hope that companies and unions, whether controlled in Canada or abroad, will act like good Canadian citizens. Indeed, as a government, we have no hesitation in saying that many do so now.
I should like to conclude with a few remarks as to the policy of the bill. In the first place, as I have already stated, it is in a sense a first step. Second, it is designed to enable the government to understand the operations of the Canadian economy, an economy which admittedly owes much and will continue to owe much to foreign investment. However, no nation which calls itself sovereign can be careless of the extent of results of foreign control of vital segments of its economy. It is essential that we should at least understand careless of the extent or results of foreign control so that we may be able sensibly to determine the policies which should be followed in order to direct our own affairs as Canadians in the kind of world in which we live.
The bill, therefore, is designed to give us two kinds of information. The information contained in part A of the returns will give us a clear picture of the extent of foreign control of the Canadian economy in both the business and the labour field. Part B of the returns will provide us with information as

to the effects of this control. It will provide to the government a picture of these effects in precise detail. The publication of the annual reports will enable the public to assess the effects at least in general outline, and so for the first time in our history, the ground will have been laid for the formulation of policy on the basis of all the facts rather than only part of them.
This brings me to the third policy consideration behind the bill. It remains a basic tenet of the Conservative party under the direction of our Prime Minister that Canadian resources should be developed and used primarily for the benefit of Canadians, and that Canadians should participate effectively in the policies which direct our economic development in order that the well-being of this and future generations of Canadians may be ensured.
We are on the threshold of exciting and challenging opportunities for Canada. We have been through difficult times and decisions. We will face equally difficult times and decisions. But surely, we as Canadians, even if we are only 18 million people, are not afraid to measure up to the challenges of new opportunities and decisions affecting our economy. What better way can we measure up to new opportunities than by formulating our policies on the basis of information as to where we now stand in reality.
This bill, then, reflects no narrow nationalistic policy. This government recognizes that we are living in a world of increasing interdependence both in terms of defence and development. We believe, however, that Canadians have a Canadian point of view to bring to bear upon that world and those developments. We believe, therefore, we can make our most effective contribution when the Canadian economy is under the effective control and direction of Canadians. We have as our objective, therefore, to co-operate with our friends both in world development as well as in national development. We expect to benefit from both spheres just as we expect them to benefit; but while we invite them to participate with us and to benefit with us in both the corporation and labour fields we do not expect them to control us; and so we intend over the years to follow policies which will have as a result the objectives set by the Prime Minister whose words I again repeat when he pronounced in the speech to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Great Britain in 1960:
We have made it clear that we expect foreign concerns operating in Canada, or Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies, to carry on operations as Canadian businesses. We expect them to make available a fair portion of their equity securities for purchase by Canadians; to include Canadians on their boards of directors; to make proper disclosure of their Canadian operations;

to employ competent Canadians in senior management and technical positions; to conduct a fair share of their research in Canada; to purchase their requirements within Canada if those are available on competitive terms; and Canadians expect not to be denied by those in control a fair opportunity to sell their Canadian products in export markets.
These policies, Mr. Speaker, we shall be able to further on the sound basis of the information that this bill will provide.

They object principally to a bill that gives the impression that cooperatives and trade unions are institutions so similar in character as to be governed by the same legislation. They say that there is a profound difference in the structure, the line of authority and objectives of a corporation and those of a trade union. Further on they say that the trade union on the contrary is a voluntary association of workers, that the right to vote is equally distributed among its members and elected officers are responsible to them; and that in short unions are associations of individuals formed for collective action in an employer-employee relationship. They further say that in the case of trade unions it is safe to say that no other institutions in Canada operate so much in the full blaze of public security. They further say that labour agrees that Bill C-38 is likely to have two effects, neither of which is desirable. They say that it will on the one hand create trouble and nuisance with respect to the provision of information, some of which is already available in one form or another and a good deal of which is of only questionable value.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the textile industry plays an important role in Canada, and indeed constitutes an economic factor of primary importance to central Canada.
In the province of Quebec, there are 417 firms employing 35,879 persons, which puts this industry in the fourth rank among Quebec manufacturing industries. A noteworthy fact is that 33.4 per cent of textile employees are female.
The principal plants are located in Sherbrooke, Magog, Drummondville, Granby,
2, 1962	2403
Tariff Board Recommendations on Textiles Shawinigan, Grand'Mere, Joliette, Three Rivers, Montmorency, Sorel, Montreal, Cow-ansville, Lachute and St. Hyacinthe.
This industry has a long history of constant progress. In 1667, Jean Talon, administrator of New France, took pride in being able to find in this country whatever garments he required. It will be recalled that, at the time, spinning and weaving were done at home.
On March 29, 1845, the first limited company in Canada started its operations at Sherbrooke, in my own constituency. That company was incorporated under the name Sherbrooke Cotton Factory.
The importance of the Canadian textile industry is revealed by the extent of Canadian investments, amounting to 80 per cent. It is therefore one of the few Canadian industries financed chiefly by Canadian capital.
Therefore, if we wish to add to our economic independence, we must protect this industry with particular care.
But especially since 1951, our textile industry has had to face many problems. I might point out that from 1951 to 1958, in the province of Quebec, the number of people it employed decreased by 10,974 and that, in the field of employment, the industry dropped from first to fifth place, all within the space of seven years. Across Canada, during the same period, 23,000 workers lost their jobs and almost 80 manufacturers had to shut down. The Canadian production of textiles, which stood at 468 million yards in 1950, had dropped to 349 million yards in 1958.
The causes of these difficulties are many and well known. Canadian production has suffered from international competition on the part of the United States and Asian countries. In 1948, 1949 and 1951, tariff reductions granted by a Liberal administration opened the door too wide to foreign products. Thus it was that, from 1950 to 1958, our textile industries lost 16 per cent of the domestic market.
Our textile products can no longer meet foreign competition, our production costs and salaries being comparatively much higher. To illustrate, here are the hourly wages in different countries: Japan, 25 cents; Italy, 51 cents; Belgium, 60 cents; Western Germany, 67 cents; United Kingdom, 80 cents; Norway and France, 86 cents; Canada, $1.34; United States, $2.
It should be noted that, while the hourly wage in the United States is $2, our neighbour, with its population of 180 million, has an enormous market, something which our 18 million people cannot provide.
2404	HOUSE OF
Tariff Board Recommendations on Textiles
When the present Progressive Conservative government came to power in the middle of 1957, the situation was already quite serious. Our textile industry was clearly on its last legs because the former Liberal government had done absolutely nothing to help it and had even taken several measures calculated to destroy it; facts and figures prove it.
To mention only a few examples, I would point out that, from 1951 to 1958, textile imports from Hong Kong increased fivefold and that those from Japan increased tenfold. In fact, the figures from the dominion bureau of statistics confirm that serious unconcern of the Liberals. In 1951, these imports from Hong Kong totalled $560,000 and from Japan, $2,555,000. In 1958, they had reached $2,597,000 and $24,023,000 respectively.
When I was elected member for Sherbrooke in 1958, I undertook, as was known to my party, to lead an active fight to restore our Canadian industry.
It is very difficult to restore to health a dying body which has too long been left without care.
But this government did tackle the task and, unlike the Liberals who had not done anything since 1945, took action in favour of our textile industry on 19 different occasions. Let me list them:
1. In 1957, the tariff board was asked to proceed with a survey and make recommendations with regard to tariffs on textiles.
2.	In 1958, the government increased the British preferential tariff on woollens and worsteds listed under item 554b of the customs tariff.
3. In 1959, the government raised the most favoured nation tariff with regard to section 554b in order to reinstate the British preferential margin.
4.	In 1958, this government substantially modified the definition of the word "dumping" for the purpose of the act.
5.	The government appointed additional assessors and provided for more detailed bills with attached samples.
6.	The government is applying measures concerning special groups of goods, on the recommendations of the tariff board, and within our international agreements.
7.	At the GATT meetings in Geneva in 1959, the government started negotiations with regard to a certain number of textiles. This action was repeated in 1960 and in 1961.


8.	The government was officially authorized to pursue those negotiations with regard to all consolidated textile items under tariff board reference No. 125.
9.	At the request of the Conservative government in August 1959, imports of textiles from Japan were temporarily stopped.
10.	On March 31, 1960, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made his budget speech and introduced four resolutions providing for a tariff raise averaging 15 per cent on foreign textile products, and especially on cotton goods.
11.	In 1960, 1961 and 1962, as requested by the Conservative government, the Japanese limited their textile exports to Canada through voluntarily applied quotas.
12.	In 1960, Mr. Fleming asked the United States to withdraw their subsidies on textile exports, but his request met with refusal.
13.	The government sought to increase the membership of the tariff board, in order that two groups may meet separately and conduct two hearings and two appeals simultaneously.
14.	In 1961, there was a new definition, in the customs tariff, of goods of a class or kind manufactured in Canada. This was to avoid undue delays in the rulings of the tariff board.
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to point out, incidentally, that the Liberal majority in the Senate blocked those last two initiatives of the present government.
15.	In the June 20, 1961 budget, the Conservative government announced new negotiations to protect the following textile products: hosiery, narrow fabrics, lace, woollen clothing and manufactured woollen goods.
16.	In October 1961, a one year treaty was
signed following the Geneva conference, in order to balance the trade in certain textile goods, while protecting our national market.
17.	The devaluation of the Canadian dollar in 1961.
18.	In 1962, our government negotiated a long term treaty providing for a better distribution of textile products throughout the world, while protecting the Canadian textile industry.
19.	In March 1962, and more especially last week, during the visit in Ottawa of the minister of economy from Hong Kong, the Canadian government prevailed upon Hong Kong to voluntarily set restrictions on certain textile goods exported to Canada.
Those 19 measures have helped to stave off a disaster and to improve the situation. In fact, foreign imports were down in 1961, and

our Canadian textile industry is picking up. A recent article on pages 1 and 2 of the Financial Post of March 17, 1962, witness to that. Here are a few extracts from this article: (Text):
There's a strong new note of optimism running through Canada's long-harassed textile industry.
Production and employment are at the highest level in five years with earnings on the rise for every major company in the industry. Several companies have just moved into the black for the first time in several years.

And a little farther on, the article adds: (Text):
Some textile officials now are forecasting an industry production gain for the year of around 10 per cent.
Competition from imports still is keen but the lower discount on our dollar-running around 6 per cent lower than this time last year-is strengthening the competitive position of local mills particularly vis-d-vis U.S. imports.

So, Mr. Speaker, it is evident that the situation is improving and that this Conservative government has done a lot to bring about an economic recovery.
However, I feel that additional steps should be taken to better set our textile industry on the road to security and prosperity. I therefore wish to offer nine suggestions to that effect:
The government should consider applying whenever necessary the provisions of section 6A of the Customs Tariff to United States subsidized cotton textiles, since Washington gave a negative answer to the request of the Canadian Minister of Finance.
Section 6A of the Customs Tariff reads as follows:
26207-1-154
Tariff Board Recommendations on Textiles Where in the opinion of the governor in council subsidized goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada have been or may be directly or indirectly imported into Canada, he may declare such goods to be subject to an additional duty on their importation equal to the amount of the subsidy on those goods as determined by him.
Japan should be asked to make public at the beginning of each year the details of its voluntary quotas thus enabling our Canadian industry to determine its production ahead of time. Moreover, those Japanese quotas should include additional items and their quantities should be reduced so as to leave a greater share for Canadian products.
Before any other delivery of grain to red China, we should ascertain that they will not try to pay us back with textile products.
The Minister of Finance should grant our textile industry certain tax concessions in order to encourage it to convert part of its production.
Section XIX of GATT should be applied, if need be, in emergencies concerning particular products.
The new definition of dumping should also be applied wherever necessary.
The government should seriously consider setting up a value for duty that would permit fairer competition between Canadian and foreign producers with respect to consumer sales.
The time has come also to set up values for duty in the case of fishing nets and Japanese-made netting.
Finally, as far as the next long term international agreement is concerned, Canada should not endorse the principle of systematic increased imports, but should strive to have the retaliation measures defined more clearly with respect to the flooding of markets by foreign products.
Those are the problems and solutions which the banking and commerce committee should consider.
That is the spirit of the resolution I have the privilege to introduce. Consequently, I would ask hon. members to express their views as to the desirability of having the said committee examine the recommendations contained in the tariff board's reports. I am speaking of the ten reports submitted by the board concerning reference 125, following the inquiry on our textile products.

Mr. Speaker, it will be seen that the motion is for a decision that in the opinion of the house consideration should be given to the advisability of referring the recommendations of

the tariff board on textiles to the standing committee on banking and commerce for the purpose of examining and reporting on the problems of the textile industry, more particularly in connection with foreign imports.

The hon. member, I take it from the purport of his remarks, intends that all the reports made by the tariff board pursuant to reference No. 125 be referred to the standing committee. If I am not correct in that, I would ask him to correct me, because the motion is not explicit in its language; but I take it that it was his intention that all the reports made on tariff board reference 125 were to be referred. On that assumption I am proceeding to discuss the matter.
I quite agree with the hon. member when he speaks about the importance of the industry in the economy of the country and when he goes on to point out the number of employees it has and the direct bearing that has on our general economy. I of course do not agree with him as to the causes or cures for the difficulties in which the industry finds itself, but I think we are on common ground that the industry has been through a very difficult period and is still in a very difficult period, and that there should be a thorough examination of those difficulties and appropriate corrective action taken to assist the industry.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) will I think agree with me on that point at least. We will, as I continue my remarks, find ourselves in disagreement, I think, as to the causes of some of the difficulties and possibly as to some of the methods of curing them. For instance, the hon. member gave certain statistics as to production in Canada and the number of employees from the year 1951 on. I have every reason to believe that his figures are correct. If they are not correct, I am not aware of any inaccuracies in them. I accept them. But he then attributed certain causes to the facts revealed by the figures. He did not, for instance, tell us that at the conclusion of the Korean war there was quite a sharp drop in the activities of the textile industry in the production of war material. That is one of the factors that slightly upsets his argument. I merely point out by way of illustrating the difficulty in choosing an arbitrary date such as 1951, when the textile industry was completing certain war production, taking that as an arbitrary date and using that figure for a comparative purpose. The point I wish to make there is that using the figures in the way he has used them does not support the arguments he made.
Then his attempt to attribute all the blame in this matter to the former government and none of the blame to the present government is just not sufficiently mature treatment of this subject and is not the kind of treatment the subject deserves. For instance, he did 26207-1-154J

Heavy taxation is undoubtedly a cost factor in the production of goods, and the failure to continue that reduction undoubtedly hurt the textile industry.
There are other factors like that which must be considered. The hon. gentleman stated that one of the factors in the present difficulty was international competition, and he was quite correct in stating that; but it is not good enough, having stated that, to blandly go on and say that the action of the government in the 12 years following the conclusion of the war in reducing taxation every year did nothing for the industry, and the action of the present government in increasing the cost of production continuously in the last five years was a great boon to the industry. That kind of argument does not treat of the subject at all. It may be listened to from some platforms, but surely it does not help in analysing the problem.
Notwithstanding what I have said on that score, I think the motion is a good one because the banking and commerce committee, if permitted to examine and report on the problems of the textile industry, could examine each one of the facets of the problem he has mentioned and the one or two I have pointed out and see exactly what effect they have had on this industry and what remedial action should be taken. The hon. member's bland assumption that tariffs are the cure-all or cause-all, depending which side of the picture you are arguing at any given moment, of these problems is just not adequate at all. Tariffs are undoubtedly a factor in this subject, and a very important factor, but they do not either cure or cause all the difficulties.
Such things as even the increase in the contributions under the Unemployment Insurance Act have a considerable effect on adding to the cost of production of textiles. The 10 per cent increase this government put on the sales tax has a great deal to do with it. The failure of the government, when these other countries the hon. member mentioned strengthened their own competitive machinery and their own economies and became strong international competitors, to recognize that and to bring our corporation tax into line with the rate of corporation tax paid by the other countries who are competitors, to examine our corporation tax, to grant larger allowances for modernization of machinery and equipment, to grant depreciation to meet that kind of problem, are all factors that are very important.

I have the impression myself-but these things would want to be examined in a more precise and detailed way-that the relief the industry needs, or a great part of it, should come out of a complete examination of our corporate tax structure, which has not been revised and is a problem that has not been faced by this government in the last five years, although these other countries with whom we compete internationally have become much more competitive in the last five years as they have built up their own economies. I think that an examination into that subject and appropriate action taken when the examination revealed, as I am sure it would, that changes are needed would do more to help this industry than any other single thing.
In any event, the point I wish to make here is that this is the kind of problem that can best be examined in a committee with witnesses in a carefully conducted hearing with an examination and, if necessary, crossexamination of those witnesses. It will be seen at once, for instance, that the administrative practices under our present corporation tax legislation are such that they do not lend themselves to easy discussion in the house in a general debate, but they would lend themselves to the most minute examination in a standing committee such as is indicated in the motion, namely the banking and commerce committee. We would see how many of these administrative practices do, in fact, unnecessarily and improperly increase the burden placed on this industry. The same comment applies to the method of computing depreciation allowances under the rules provided by the income tax legislation, as well as the legislation fixing the rates of taxation itself.
There are, of course, many problems here. It was interesting for instance, to hear the hon. member point out that one of our main competitors in this industry was the United States. Then a few moments later in his interesting remarks he drew attention to the fact that the highest hourly wage rate paid in the industry was paid in the United States, the very country which provides us with such strong competition. The wage rate there per hour is eight times the wage rate paid in the industry in Japan and it is something like 50 per cent higher than the rate paid in Canada. The rate varies widely, of course in various countries. In West Germany, for instance, it is about one third of that paid in the United States. Questions of this kind could be examined in committee to see what these different wage rates have to do with the problem and to what extent there should be compensatory legislation to protect


the high standard of living in this country which I think all hon. members wish to see protected.
The point I wish to make out of all this is
that in my view this is a problem which should go to a committee of members for examination. I believe the banking and commerce committee is the appropriate committee. I think the condition of the industry is such that remedial action is needed. As a matter of fact, if I were to follow that part of the hon. member's contribution in which he was making a political speech I would be critical of the government for not having taken remedial action sooner. This problem is an urgent one and it should be dealt with now. I wish to make it clear, therefore that I should like to see this motion carried and, when it has been carried, see an appropriate motion put on the order paper to refer the subject to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, you will remember that, during the summer and fall of last year, our friends opposite were trying to sow seeds of confusion among the people, by making a great fuss about the alarming unemployment situation at the time. Therefore, being interested to know the exact working conditions in our local industries, I took it upon myself to visit the various plants in the city of St. Hyacinthe.
