Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock, when I had to interrupt my remarks, I was saying that the unions are not at all satisfied with the bill in its present form.
I understand that they did not strongly oppose this bill, but they did oppose it clearly enough, and that opposition is worth mentioning. Mr. Speaker, I will say frankly that I did not mention all the things that the brief contains about this Bill C-38 because it would have taken too much time.
I see, in the last part, the following:
(Text):
There is none the less a good deal of detailed criticism of the bill which the congress would like to make and feels it should have the right to make, but this is not the appropriate place or occasion. We strongly urge that the congress and other interested parties be given an opportunity to make formal representations, either to a parliamentary committee or otherwise, before the bill is enacted.
(Translation):
That was just what we were asking for, and what the unions are asking at this time. And I am convinced that a number of corporations only want, as do the unions, to have an opportunity of explaining their position and stating clearly what they disapprove in this bill.
As I said in my opening remarks, the basic principle of the bill is not bad, but it was badly prepared. It is a bill with several faulty sections. We should be given the opportunity of discussing them in committee.
No need to be a lawyer to realize at a glance that the bill needs improving. Indeed, the minister himself said that "We prepared several amendments which will be submitted by my colleagues." Since he introduced the bill in the house, he discovered the need for some improvement, it means he admits that, in principle, the bill is imperfect and incomplete.
Now, in agreement with the Canadian congress of labour, as well as with others I had the opportunity of meeting, we want to ask the minister to avoid all excessive hurry when discussing the bill, and to refer it rather to the standing committee on industrial relations, so that people who have some information to give, or objection to raise, may do so. As a matter of fact, that is the only democratic way to proceed, but that is not the policy of this government.
If the people concerned have not been advised beforehand, how can they express
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Chown).]

their views in the house since in the committee of the whole, nobody but a member may rise and speak? Therefore, this is done at the expense of those primarily concerned.
I believe a staff of experts should be appointed who would see to the preparing of reports and have an opportunity of enlightening the house. How many experts on this matter are there here? Not many, I would say.
Now, that is the reason why we need the help of those who are more particularly affected by the bill.
We might hear experts on constitutional matters who would tell us how they interpret the bill. We might also have representatives of corporations who would state what form they would like the bill to have to be of any help to them. And, finally, we could have experts in industrial relations who would explain the various ways to deal with labour matters.
Besides, the bill itself should not have been introduced as one bill; there should have been two different bills: one for corporations and one for labour unions. In fact, if we examine the situation closely, it is easy to see that the views, purposes and even wishes of corporations differ from those of labour unions. Consequently, the two should always be dealt with separately.
But, to speed things up before the election, the minister has introduced a bill which is incomplete and ill-conceived, as will be shown at the committee stage.
I suggest that the bill is a dangerous one.
The minister stated a while ago that the bill was divided in two parts, one having to do with statistical and non-confidential information, the other with confidential information.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how the minister can still believe that by virtue of some provision of this bill, secrecy cannot be violated, after he has prepared it himself or with his experts.
You only need to read it to know that secrecy cannot be safeguarded, since according to the definitions in it, any person who is or has been employed by the government could ask for and obtain information, and nobody could prevent him from getting it. Besides, a former employee of a company could come today and ask for information and you could not turn him down, according to the wording of this bill.

Now, we claim that there have been and still may be some people so interested in money that they could sell themselves to a company in order to obtain some information about a competitor. Such people could obtain information which they could sell or give away.
Some will say: They are federal civil servants and you usually defend them. That is true but there might be some among them in whom you could not place your confidence. We might find some odd individuals willing to sell information available to them. That does not mean that the civil service is bad. Indeed, Christ had one Judas among his twelve apostles and you would not say that the others did not deserve his confidence.
Mr. Speaker, this bill contains numerous provisions which could not be accepted before they have been considered by a standing committee of the house where experts could advise us on how to improve them.
For example, somewhere in the bill provision is made for a maximum term of imprisonment and a maximum fine, but no minimum is stated. In short, if the judge is lenient, he could sentence the accused to a five cent fine or an hour in jail.
That is why I tell you that it is too late to introduce this bill in the house, the more so because it is impossible to study it in full and adequately.
A while ago the minister said that the bill is introduced under section 91 of the British North America Act. Well, I ask the minister to find, in Bill No. C-38 that he is introducing today, a section that says clearly that this measure is introduced under section 91 of the British North America Act.
I am convinced that this bill represents a constitutional hazard.
Can companies or unions of a purely provincial nature be forced to answer questions for any purpose other than taxation? If they refuse to do so, how can the minister compel them to answer?
Besides, I do not regard that provision as very important, for the corporations and even the unions will be able to defend themselves when the time comes. Nevertheless, there is always a danger. If the minister had really wanted the bill to be in accordance with clause 91 of the British North America Act, he should have prepared a preamble in which he would have specified it. It should have been not only stated, but written.
We are being asked to accept and sign a blank cheque. We are simply being asked to allow civil servants to ask all the questions they like, without those questions having been submitted to the house.

Corporations and Labour Unions
Had the minister wanted to make this bill more complete, he should have added to it an appendix giving a form, a sample of the questions, so as to show which questions will be asked.
Now, I will be told that a certain part of those things are defined in the bill. But what we want to know is the nature of the questionnaires which will be sent to the industrialists, the representatives of the corporations, of the trade unions, in short, to whoever information will be sought from.
In my opinion, as long as we do not have these forms, it is wrong to ask the house to approve such an incomplete bill.
I could have introduced an amendment to have the bill referred to a standing committee of this house, but it would have killed it. It would have been a non-confidence motion. But that is not our purpose; we want the bill to be studied further.
We feel that the government is entitled to ask information from all corporations operating in Canada; it has the right to know how the union funds are used. But to that end, we believe that the bill should be referred to a committee in order to make it a complete and acceptable bill.
This bill is not too bad, but the drafting is poor. It comes too late, at the end of a session, at the end of a parliament.
We know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) have had that project in mind for quite a while, because it was mentioned as early as 1957.
In 1960, the Prime Minister made a statement to that effect in England.
Well, if they were thinking about it at the time, why wait until April 1962, at the end of a session, at the end of a parliament, when we know quite well that even if that measure is adopted it will have no effect for some time, because they will need time to gather information.
If the bill had been introduced two months later, that would have made no difference, save that the public could have had the time to prepare itself.
Therefore, I once again urge the minister to kindly refer the bill to the standing committee on industrial relations, in order that the people concerned may democratically exercise their right to express their views, to submit briefs and evidence, which would also permit us to have before the committee economists who could enlighten us on the

Corporations and Labour Unions various phases oi this bill because it includes several sections we shall have to consider. Furthermore, I would ask him to grant the request made by the Canadian congress of labour in its brief dated March 14, 1962.
Once again, I would ask the minister to refer the bill to the standing committee on industrial relations in order that it may be seriously considered, so that, at least, when it is returned to the house, it might be clear enough for the corporations, as well as the unions, to know what they have to offer and what the government expects from them.

The first and most important objection is the one that has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Hull. It is the one that is spoken of in the brief which the Canadian Labour Congress presented to the government a couple of weeks ago. I refer to the attempt in this bill to lump together as one class and kind, to use a favourite expression of the government, and as being the same or similar, corporations, co-operatives and trade unions; trying to create in the public mind the image that these are all one and the same thing.
I would like to say that this cannot be done by the mere passing of a bill. Certainly with the majority this government possesses at the present time they could pass a bill saying that moose and wolves were the same, but that would not make it so. The same thing applies to this bill. If and when the bill is passed, it certainly is not going to make corporations, trade unions and co-operatives one and the same thing. Corporations and trade unions are not the same; they cannot be the same, and they will not be the same even when this bill passes and becomes law.
I would like to deal briefly with some of the reasons why this is so. Apparently government members do not realize this or they would not be trying to lump them together under one umbrella in this bill. Corporations have one motive and one motive only. It is clearcut and it is simple. Their motive is to make money. They are not benevolent societies; they would not be in business if they were. Corporations long ago realized that for their present and future benefit they should take political action. This they have done for many years in connection with the two old line parties. This is something that the trade unions are only now learning, and it is something the co-operatives have still to learn.

I think that if we check back through history we will find that no law that has ever been passed by a Liberal or Conservative government has interfered too much with corporations.
Co-operatives, on the other hand, are slightly more complicated. They are groups of people with certain common interests, working together-I almost said "collectively", but that is a bad word; that is one of the words that unfortunately the communists have banished from our dictionaries-but working together for the common good; they combine the basic motive of gain of the corporation with the basic motive of protection from exploitation which is common in the trade unions.
I am not discussing the merits of these various things but I would just like to point out the differences between them and the reason why we should not try and group them all together, as is being done in this bill.
Trade unions, on the other hand, are much more complicated than the other two. First of all their main motive is protection, and the only reason they came about was to protect themselves from the exploitation by the corporations. So they cannot be one and the same thing. I am one of those who think that we have in this country far too much of trade unions versus management, instead of trade unions with management. I think that before we can ever hope for a rosy future we have to take a different look from that which we

Trade unions, the same as any other group in our society, are subject to our laws. After all, labour laws, like all laws, were written by governments, which I have already stated have in the main been responsible to the corporations. They are the only government we have ever had in this country.
Trade unions also have the motive of personal gain. In this respect only are they like corporations. They also have something in common with co-operatives, because through their efforts benefits accrue not only to themselves but to society as a whole. Trade unions were built by two different kinds of people. You have the idealists, people who work all their lives for something in which they believe, and you have the professionals who work for something for which they are paid. Originally they were all idealists, but unfortunately the trade union movement found that it was up against a loaded deck. It is pretty difficult to fight with a bunch of idealists on one side and a bunch of professionals on the other, and therefore the trade unions have had to turn more and more to professions in order to meet them. I should like to point out another disparity in the treatment afforded to these two different groups which are thrown together in this way. We find that the penalties, fines, prison terms and so on are equal for each side. In other words, they are identical. But I should like to compare the gross revenues involved for each of these two groups. As one example, I should like to take a case with which I am familiar-the Hollinger gold mine. There are about 800 men in the bargaining unit and at a current rate of $5 a month union dues, if the members were all paying dues, which they are not, this would amount to a gross of $48,000 a year. In 1959, the mine produced 205,727 ounces of gold. If we use the round figure of $35 an ounce, that amounts to some $7,200,465. In the same year the company received emergency gold mining assistance amounting to $817,663, making a total gross revenue of $8,018,128. So we find a gross of more than $8 million on one hand versus a maximum of $48,000 on the other. Nevertheless the penalties for the infringement of this bill are identical in both cases. This certainly is the case of the stew with the one horse and one rabbit in equal parts.
One aspect of this bill could, I feel, be very dangerous, particularly in areas such as the one from which I come, where there is no union security and no check-off of dues. In a situation like this one has to run pretty well as a bluff for most of the year, and in many cases if the operators or the companies were to realize how low the membership might drop in a trade union at a given period when there is no check-off of dues it might lead to all kinds of trouble.
A further aspect of the bill with which I nust find fault is its discriminatory aspects. Why is nationality rather than citizenship asked for in this bill? Why, when a report on 

membership is given, must there be discrimination between male and female members? Surely a union member is a union member regardless of sex or nationality. There is another part of this bill which I find amusing. It puzzled me for a while but finally I have found a solution. In his little book entitled "An Uninhibited History of Canada", the author, Professor Eric Nicol, refers to the bill of rights as follows:
Included in the bill of rights are all the freedoms that Canadians hold precious, except freedom from under-arm perspiration. It states that everybody is entitled to a lawyer unless it is perfectly obvious that he is guilty (e.g. communists, sex fiends, Liberals, C.C.F. and off-duty postal clerks).
I think we could add a couple more classifications to that. I think we could add corporations and trade unions, because in certain provisions of this bill we find words to the effect that if they are guilty of an offence the penalties will apply regardless of whether they have been tried or convicted. I think this would fit very well into Professor Nicol's description of our bill of rights.
I have spent a good deal more time dealing with the bad points in this bill than I have with the good points but, as I have said before, my experience in this house is that supporters of the government have always been oblivious to the bad points and therefore these need greater stress.
Just before he ended his remarks, the minister mentioned something about the fact that the government wanted to gather all the information it could with regard to corporations and trade unions. But he has completely ignored something which is of vital concern to this country. In the last two or three years we have heard a great deal of criticism, especially by the newspapers and by members on the government side of this house regarding trade union support of the New Democratic party. We have also heard criticism from time to time about political support of the two old line parties by corporations. If we really want to know all the facts, taking the minister at his word that he really wishes to have all the information that is available, I am surprised that this aspect was not considered when the bill was being prepared. Mr. Speaker, as one who has had a private member's bill on the order paper for the last three or four years dealing with financial disclosure by Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies I am naturally interested in this bill. I must give the government full marks for having gone much further than my bill in certain respects, in that the government has included in this measure all companies in Canada both public and private, whether operating under federal or provincial charter; and labour unions are also brought in under this umbrella. I was rather surprised that the minister did not refer to previous debates in this house on my bill because I think those debates were quite informative and would have been of assistance to the minister's staff in the drafting of this measure.
Frankly, I have somewhat mixed feelings about this bill. It represents a step forward but it does not seem to me to go far enough. It appears to me that the information contained in part A is the type of information which, although it cannot be described as inconsequential, does not amount to very much. It is not the type of information that varies from year to year.
Why there should be a fee for this information I do not know. I think the fee might well be removed. It is supposed to cover the cost of indexing and that sort of thing. There will have to be facilities set up to do this if we are to receive tables and reports, and so

this cost is there from the beginning. It might be good policy to eliminate the fee.
I was interested in the statement made by the minister with regard to outside control of Canadian industry. This was brought out in previous discussions in the bill to which I referred. It is an amazing fact that a highly developed industrial nation like Canada stands in the position it does. It stands in that position because we have had to have massive imports of foreign capital to develop this country. We needed and wanted this capital; it has been welcome. As the minister said, capital has certain responsibilities to this country, as well as rights. We offer a stable political climate, except perhaps in the province of British Columbia, where capital can develop, where capital can gain the advantages of development in our resource industries. We offer good markets. We offer an access, up to now anyway, to commonwealth markets. We have many advantages for foreign capital and foreign capital comes here not to do us a favour but because it is a good climate for foreign capital. In this respect I take strong exception to what was said by the hon. member for Hull who seems to think that the favour is being done to us when foreign capital comes here. It is a favour on both sides. The extent of this capital is well illustrated in "The Canadian Balance of International Payments, 1960," put out by the dominion bureau of statistics. On page 60, statement 32, "Ownership and Control of Selected Canadian Industries," we find here that, with respect to the rubber industry, in 1959, 98 per cent of it was under foreign control; pulp and paper in 1959, 49 per cent under foreign control; agricultural machinery, 55 per cent; automobiles and parts, 97 per cent; transportation equipment, 73 per cent; electrical apparatus, 81 per cent; chemicals, 77 per cent.
I should like also to refer to the autumn issue of Queen's Quarterly for 1958 in which is found an article by Professor J. E. Smyth entitled "Financial Disclosures by Subsidiaries". This is what Professor Smyth had to say about this matter, and this has to do with what is properly secret information and what is properly public information. I quote:
But the concept of what information is private is somehow related to the concept of what property is private. Those who are sensitive about their property rights are likely also to have precise ideas about what business is their own and no one else's. The ownership of property implies the right to exclude all others from a knowledge of its use (as long as the use is lawful) and of the results of its use. The problem today, however, is to decide in what sense the property of large business is private, and if it is private, who is entitled to the amenities of such privacy. The assets of large corporations are financed by shareholders and by creditors (including employees who must wait

for payment until they have rendered their services) . Public relations programs are designed to convince the consumer that he too has a stake in the corporation.
And so it goes on. In referring to disclosure of information, at pages 404 and 405 Professor Smyth had this to say:
What we have in Canada today is a distracting unevenness in the publication of financial information.
He states:
It is when some businesses disclose their financial affairs and condition with candour and others (equally large) are allowed to maintain an inscrutable silence that we can never know where we stand, and that some businesses may enjoy, unfairly, such advantage as there may be in secrecy.
The minister made quite a play on that point. He mentioned that this disclosure could be damaging competitively, that it could be of immense value to competitors. What is the minister talking about? The minister is talking about foreign owned subsidiaries in competition with Canadian companies. This is the way I read it. So we want to perpetuate this advantage, if there is an advantage in secrecy, to the foreign company as compared with the Canadian company. What are these foreign companies? I can give a short list of some of them. They include such companies as the Borden Company, Bristol Myers of Canada, Campbell Soup, Canadian International Paper, Chrysler Corporation, Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive, General Foods, General Mills, General Motors, H. J. Heinz, International Harvester, Irone Ore Company of Canada, Kellogg Company, Kraft Foods, Nabisco Foods, and National Cash Register. There is a whole galaxy of major corporations across this country, with one exception.
I mentioned International Harvester. In one session when my bill was being debated and I mentioned the name of International Harvester Company, I received a letter from the president of International Harvester stating that although International Harvester was a fully owned subsidiary of a United States company, they felt it their duty to their customers and to their employees in Canada to make full and complete disclosure of the Canadian operations and they were putting out a balance sheet, profit and loss statements and all the rest of the financial papers which are supposed to be put out by a public company in Canada. They said they were doing this so they would take the people of Canada into their confidence as to what they were doing. I say that this is an enlightened management when that sort of thing is done. But that is not done too often.
What are we asking for, or what were we asking for before this bill was amended? Again, according to Professor Smyth at page 408:

The third point made by the Prime Minister was proper disclosure. I fail to see why information which the parent company puts out in the United States-and we are talking mainly about United States subsidiaries as they have the great bulk of investment in this country-or financial statements should be in part B. I can see good reason for much of the information being asked for being in part B.

I go back to Professor Smyth, Mr. Speaker, where he says:
One of the unfortunate by-products of the present situation, quite apart from its larger implications, is that research in the field of business finance in Canada is stymied at many points because of the large blind spots in our knowledge of what is taking palce in the Canadian economy. The incidence of the operations of subsidiaries upon the Canadian economy is so great that one can never be sure that such published financial statements as we do receive give a typical picture of economic trends and financial developments in Canada. Until about four years ago the Bank of Canada compiled and published financial data from a sample of Canadian companies; it has since abandoned the series. One of the important limitations of these data was that they were drawn entirely from published financial statements, and that the proportion of Canadian economic activity which was affected by large private companies, for which no statements were available, was so significant as to invalidate any conclusions which might be drawn from the published figures.

Most of the representations to the government about the structure of the bill last year were from corporations or interests operating on behalf of corporations, and the bill before us now implements most of their suggestions. I might be unfair if I were to say that the minister knuckled under to these representations. Perhaps it would be more accurate to say this is what he wanted to do in the first place, but he did not know how to have the bill drafted so it would meet the desires of the corporations in this country.
I do not think the minister dealt with the bill itself to any great extent because his remarks were interlarded with references to economic independence and to the development of a Canadian identity so far as corporation and union structures were concerned. He made quite a few references to national development, to ownership, control and utilization of our own resources, all of which are very commendable ideals and are very worthwhile things for the minister to express, but
Corporations and Labour Unions these are not the things which the bill specifies. It does not deal with these questions at all. It deals entirely and exclusively with the filing of statistics about the operations of corporations and unions, albeit arising from that information someone will discover the degree to which corporations and unions have international affiliations or have international controls exercised over them.
Apparently the bill is based upon a speech made by the Prime Minister to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Great Britain, during which he made reference to a number of things he would like to see existing in Canada with regard to foreign controls and foreign concerns. The Prime Minister said:
We expect to make available a fair portion of their equity securities for purchase by Canadians:
This is something highly commendable. We would all like to see more opportunities provided for Canadian financiers to participate in the operation and formation of companies, be they foreign or otherwise; but the bill says nothing about that. The Prime Minister also said that we expect them "to include Canadians on their boards of directors". Are we to balance that statement of the Prime Minister, which stated one of his great national goals was to have Canadians on boards of directors, against this piece of legislation? Were we to do that we could say that we do not believe the Prime Minister because the bill does not propose to carry out what the Prime Minister hoped would be effected.
Your Honour will remember that last session we spent hour after hour after hour until finally, after what seemed an interminably long time, we were able to get one small pipe line company, Aurora pipe lines, in the position of having Canadians as its directors. We had to put up a long battle to achieve that objective, an objective which was in concert with the attitude expressed by the Prime Minister. However the bill before us does not cover that point at all.
The Prime Minister also said he wanted foreign concerns "to make proper disclosure of their Canadian operations." The hon. member for Vancouver South, who has just spoken, said this bill does not allow for the making of proper disclosures. It allows for the making of certain disclosures but, as pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver South, who has studied this question

Corporations and Labour Unions at great length, the bill is worthless in that regard because it does not provide tor the making of proper disclosure.

The suggestion has been made that the bill is defective because somehow or other it seeks to equate the corporations and the trade unions. I can only say that anyone who studies the bill will realize how ill founded is this criticism. Of course, it is not the purpose or the effect of this bill to make them the same; the sole purpose is to require both to report statistics. There is no other purpose, and I cannot see, on the basis of the arguments so far advanced, how anyone can suggest that there is anything improper in requiring the two types of organization to make returns in the one piece of legislation. That does not seem to me to indicate in any way that we are trying to equate the operations of trade unions and corporations. One has heard suggestions that we should get on with the business of the session. With that, I quite agree. Yet hon. members on the other side seem to suggest that instead of doing this thing efficiently and expeditiously by providing in the same piece of legislation for these returns, we should take further time in the house by introducing two separate pieces of legislation.
Further, the suggestion was made that the bill was defective in that the penalties provided for infringement are the same in respect to both corporations and unions. This criticism, again, surprised me. I can only point out in answer that this is a universal principle with respect to legislation. The principle is that penalties for the breach of a statute should be the same no matter who commits that breach. Does the hon. member who made that criticism really mean to imply what is inherent in his criticism, namely that there should be one law for the powerful and another for the weak? Certainly that has never been in my opinion a proper basis on which to found any provision setting forth a penalty for breach of statute.
The fact is that what we desire to acquire is information about the activities of those who control from outside certain elements of the Canadian economy, whether that control be exercised in the field of corporation activity or of trade union activity. So we have provided without discrimination that

both segments of the economy should be required to make returns and be subject to the same penalty if there is any breach of the statute.
My hon. friend from Vancouver South made an interesting and constructive speech. It was pointed out by him that he has had bills on the order paper in previous sessions having as their object a similar purpose to that of this bill. That is true, and I should like to express my appreciation to him both for his interest in the subject and the contribution and studies he has made of it, also for the fact that he reminded me that I did not refer to those efforts in my introductory remarks. If there be any omission for which I should be blamed, I accept the criticism gladly. The hon. member for Vancouver South put on record a number of statistics with respect to the extent of foreign ownership and I am sure he will agree with me that these reinforce the arguments in favour of this bill, arguments which suggest that it is timely now that we should take steps to determine the effect and extent of this foreign ownership. I appreciate that the hon. gentleman feels the bill is defective, in that it provides that much of the financial information to be submitted in the returns should be kept confidential. This is because as a result of the consideration we gave after Bill No. C-70 was introduced last session we decided that the representations made with respect to the discriminatory aspects of that bill were well founded. Accordingly, we decided that in the new bill introduced this session we should require the same kind of information to be filed, but by all companies whether private or public and whether Canadian owned or foreign controlled. Having made that decision, the point my hon. friend makes that it preserves somehow the competitive advantage of foreign companies to keep that information confidential is, I submit, not well taken. If
Corporations and Labour Unions my hon. friend will give due weight to the effect of what this bill requires, he will realize that all companies are now required to report. This includes, for instance, Canadian private companies, and these private companies are required to make returns under this bill which they are not otherwise required to make available to the public. Therefore, for us to have allowed that these returns might become public knowledge would have had the effect that information regarding the operations of Canadian private companies, to single out this one group, would have been available to their competitors, including foreign owned United States competitors, to the great advantage of those competitors.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, no one would suggest that we should take any action which would increase what my hon. friend has said is a competitive advantage already existing in favour of foreign owned companies. No, our conclusion was that because it is desirable that the government should obtain this information from all companies, including Canadian owned as well as foreign controlled, and private as well as public companies, that consideration outweighed the consideration in favour of making this information available in detail to the public; because to do so would place Canadian companies which now have the benefit of privacy with respect to certain of their operations at a disadvantage; would place that information at the disposal of their competitors who are controlled from outside the country and thus give their competitors an advantage which at the moment they do not have. We do not feel that these details of the operation of Canadian companies in the category I have mentioned should be exposed to their United States competitors.
As I said in opening the debate on second reading, we recognize that the bill is to an extent experimental, that this is a first step. It is a step that has never been taken before. As a result of this bill, the government, for the first time in our history, will be in possession of all the facts as to the operation of our economy, the influence on that economy of control of important segments exercised from outside the country; and by having the advantage of the information with respect to both Canadian owned and controlled organizations as well as the foreign owned and controlled organizations we can compare the facts and see the full impact on our economy of these foreign controlled operations, whether it be in the corporation or the union field. We can then, as a result of that information, assess the situation and base specific policies, either administrative or legislative, which we will present in the future, upon an intelligent

Corporations and Labour Unions appreciation of all the facts instead of upon conjecture, prejudice or only a partial appreciation of the facts.
This bill will enable us to develop policy in the field of ensuring effective Canadian control of the Canadian economy and, of course, the information it places at our disposal will also enable us to remedy any defects which may be disclosed as time goes on. In other words, we recognize this as an important step, but a first step, an experimental measure which time and experience may indicate requires certain amendments or modifications. We will be prepared to introduce those modifications on the basis of experience. I am convinced, however, that this step is so important that it is well justified in spite of any uncertainties or risks. Let me make clear that we are not uncertain as to our policy; I mean uncertainty only as to the very best and final way to go about implementing it. Nevertheless the objective to be accomplished in terms of ensuring control by Canadians of the Canadian economy is so important that any risks are well justified. I feel experience will show that this is one of the most important and far reaching steps, in terms of true national development and national policy, that any government has yet taken.

The regulation of trade and commerce.

Consequently, there seems to be some conflict, which could have been avoided if the minister had included in his bill a preamble in these words; "This bill has been drawn up under the authority of section 91, subsection 1, paragraph 2, of the British North America Act".

I think that would have made it much more acceptable from a constitutional point of view.

It seems to me that this is an answer to the hon. member's suggestion that we should insert a preamble defining, as I understood him to say, precisely the provision upon which we rely. Certainly we do not rely precisely or exclusively on the trade and commerce heading. As I said, heading 6 appeals to us. However, I think there are others. There are also general provisions upon which we rely with respect to federal jurisdiction. I think it would be extremely unwise in a bill of this sort to attempt to define with particularity precisely the constitutional grounds upon which we rely as to the validity of the legislation. In saying that I do not mean to imply that we have not examined the point with precision and particularity. We have done so and we are satisfied that this bill is within the constitutional authority of parliament.
With regard to the amendments referred to by the hon. member for Skeena may I say that the consequential amendments, while they may be fairly numerous, are minor in nature. I can give him and the committee that assurance. They are changes in the designation of the minister and of officials holding responsibility arising largely out of the decision to entrust the dominion bureau of statistics with responsibility for the reception in the first place of these returns, and the custody of part B. The amendments to all the other portions of the act arise out of the major amendments to clause 14. The amendment to clause 14 affects the definition of official persons and their conduct in connection with the custody of information that comes to them. It does not in itself have very many consequential amendments. The consequential amendments derive mainly from the decision to give the bureau of statistics custody, as I have said. I therefore do not really think there is any necessity for anticipating the amendment to clause 14 at this stage.

speechtext: Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the house leader could indicate the urgent and important business the government proposes to bring before us tomorrow and each succeeding day of this week so that the opposition will be well prepared to expedite that business.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
All government business is important. May I stress that fact. Of course it is also urgent. Otherwise it would not be before hon. members. The first item tomorrow will be the bill based on the resolution which was passed today dealing with amendments to the Judges Act and then we will carry on in the committee stage with Bill No. C-38 which we have just been considering. Then we will follow with the resolution
in the name of the Prime Minister dealing with the electoral boundaries commission. Then we shall take second reading of Bill No. S-19, to amend the Canada Grain Act. That appears to be the order in which these items will be taken tomorrow.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: May I ask the house leader if we can be reasonably sure there will not be a change of program, that the Prime Minister will proceed with the resolution, and that this indication of urgency would mean that redistribution is to take place before there is an election?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: There are far too many questions here. However, in view of the tremendous burdens which fall upon a prime minister, I am sure the house would be perfectly agreeable to any shift in the order of business to accommodate him. It is just normal.
